main.t: A single midline bone between the orbits that forms the roof and upper walls of the nasal cavity (ethmoid bone).

simpler.t: The ethmoid bone sits behind the top of your nose, between your eyes.

deeper.t: The nerve fibres for smell pass through its cribriform plate into the brain.

facts.t: It lies in the midline, between the orbit and the upper nasal cavity on each side.
Inside the skull, it forms a small midline area of the floor of the anterior cranial fossa.
It forms the upper nasal septum and part of the medial wall of each orbit.

simpler.t: It is deep behind the bridge of your nose, between your eye sockets.

deeper.t: Though counted with the brain case, it also helps form the nasal septum, nasal walls and orbits.

items.name: Crista galli
items.t: A small upward projection in the midline (“rooster’s comb”). It anchors one of the coverings of the brain.

items.name: Cribriform plates
items.t: Flat plates either side of it (“sieve”), pierced by small olfactory foramina.

items.name: Perpendicular plate
items.t: Forms the upper part of the nasal septum.

items.name: Superior and middle nasal conchae
items.t: Thin curved plates projecting from each side wall of the nasal cavity.

items.name: Ethmoid air cells
items.t: Many small air spaces with very thin walls, between the nasal cavity and the orbit.

items.name: Orbital surface
items.t: Forms much of the medial wall of each orbit, with the lacrimal bone.

simpler.t: It has a sieve-like roof, a central plate in the nose and two scroll-like plates on each side.

deeper.t: The superior concha is the smallest; it is hidden above and behind the middle concha.

facts.t: Its cribriform plates are pierced by olfactory foramina, letting the fibres for smell reach the brain.
Its curved conchae swirl incoming air, helping to warm and moisten it.
Mucus on the conchae traps dust, pollen, bacteria and viruses.
Its air cells are part of the paranasal sinuses, which lighten the skull.

simpler.t: It lets the nerves for smell through, and helps warm and clean the air you breathe.

items.name: Olfactory nerve
items.t: Its fibres pass from the nasal lining through the cribriform plate to the olfactory bulb.

items.name: Frontal lobe
items.t: The olfactory bulb lies on its underside, just above the cribriform plate.

items.name: Vomer
items.t: With the perpendicular plate and the septal cartilage, forms the nasal septum.

items.name: Lacrimal bone
items.t: Together they form much of the medial wall of the orbit.

items.name: Frontal bone
items.t: Forms most of the floor of the anterior cranial fossa, around the ethmoid’s small midline part.

items.name: Covering of the brain
items.t: One of the layers covering the brain is anchored to the crista galli.

simpler.t: The nerves for smell pass through it to the brain, and it joins the bones of the nose and orbit.

facts.t: Like the bones of the skull base and face, it forms from a cartilage model (endochondral ossification).
The paranasal sinuses, including its air cells, enlarge during childhood.

items.injury: Blunt force to the face, as in a car accident.
items.damaged: The olfactory nerve fibres are sheared where they pass through the cribriform plate.
items.why: The frontal lobe moves relative to the ethmoid bone, tearing the fine fibres.

items.injury: A fracture through the cribriform plate.
items.damaged: The coverings of the brain over the plate tear.
items.cannotDo: Keep the nose dry: the clear fluid around the brain (cerebrospinal fluid) leaks from the nose.
items.why: The thin plate is all that separates the nasal cavity from the cranial cavity.
items.check: Leakage of cerebrospinal fluid from the nose is not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20); the plate’s position is.

items.q: Explain how a blow to the face can cause loss of smell.
model: Olfactory nerve fibres pass through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone.
They reach the olfactory bulb on the underside of the frontal lobe.
In a blow, the frontal lobe moves relative to the ethmoid bone.
The fibres are sheared, causing anosmia.

items.q: Compare the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid with the vomer.
model: Both form part of the bony nasal septum.
The perpendicular plate forms its upper part.
The triangular vomer forms its lower and back parts.
Septal cartilage fills the gap between them at the front.

items.q: Predict which nasal conchae you would see looking into the front of a dry skull, and explain why.
model: The inferior concha is the largest.
The middle concha, part of the ethmoid, lies just above it.
The small superior concha is hidden above and behind the middle one.

check.stem: What passes through the cribriform plate?
check.why: Olfactory axons pass through the olfactory foramina of the cribriform plate.

check.stem: Which nasal conchae are part of the ethmoid bone?
check.why: The superior and middle conchae belong to the ethmoid; the inferior concha is a separate bone.

check.stem: What does the crista galli anchor?
options: One of the coverings of the brain
check.why: It is an anterior attachment point for one of the covering layers of the brain.
